items.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025
items.q: if he wanted a certain note in the bass he would just hit it. He would just bang-bang-bang-bang — I’d say okay, you got it.

ctx.x: Did any of these artists ever tell you to stop doing something? Or to suggest that why don’t you play this this way. Give you some instruction?

The only one was — I think it was Ahmad. Because he — and he didn’t do it that much. You know he had a different way of — he didn’t play songs the way other people did. He always altered the changes, he always, you know used substitutions. And his substitutions were his own and so you had to learn that from him. You had to learn them. And a lot of times I would hear them, sometimes if I didn’t he would you know — and see he didn’t do a lot of verbalization in terms of do this, do that, he would just — if he…

being flexible — I remember one time we were — I was working with Abbey Lincoln at the Village Vanguard. And we already had been playing around, the band sounded pretty good. But on the first set of the Village Vanguard we were — she felt like anyway — like the band was a little tight, you know, a little edgy. So she turns around after the first two songs and she says — and the people could hear it too ‘cause the mic was on. She says, “Listen, don’t worry because this is The Vanguard, this is the easiest place to…
